\chapter{The Clock}
\label{ch:mr-ghadyal}
\hlchaptermodality{67}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask what time it is, say what time it is, and say that something happens at a given hour.}

From cold: ask the time, tell it with the verb that counts, and place an event at an hour with the form that never changes.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kitī vājle]{\mr{किती} \mr{वाजले} (kitī vājle) — \textquotedblleft{}what time is it?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C67-vajle}



\begin{quote}
Count from one to five. Then say the word you use to ask \emph{how many}.

You already own both halves of this chapter's question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{किती} \mr{वाजले}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{वाजले}?} — \emph{kitī vājle?} — \textbf{what time is it?}
\end{quote}

The question word is \textbf{\mr{किती}}, the one you ask \emph{how many} with. Marathi does not ask \emph{what} time it is — it asks \textbf{how many have sounded.}

\textbf{\mr{वाजणे}} is to sound, to ring, to strike. English kept that picture when clocks had bells — \emph{the clock struck three}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb counts with you}]
Answer it with a number, and \textbf{the verb changes for one}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{वाजला}.} \emph{ek vājlā} & It is one o'clock. \\
\textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजले}.} \emph{don vājle} & It is two o'clock. \\
\textbf{\mr{पाच} \mr{वाजले}.} \emph{pāc vājle} & It is five o'clock. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{One struck. Two struck.} Singular for one, plural for everything above it, which is what a verb about \emph{how many sounded} ought to do.

You have seen a Marathi verb go plural before, in \textbf{\mr{तुम्ही} \mr{कसे} \mr{आहात}} — but that plural was for \textbf{respect}, on one person. This one is plural because the things counted really are more than one. Same shape, different reason.

So there is one form to learn, not twelve: \textbf{-\mr{ला}} after \mr{एक}, \textbf{-\mr{ले}} after every other number.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kitī vājle?}
  \item \emph{ek vājlā} — one o'clock
  \item \emph{don vājle}, \emph{tīn vājle}, \emph{chār vājle}
  \item which number is the odd one out, and what it does to the verb
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the question literally ask? (\textbf{How many have sounded}.) Which number takes \textbf{\mr{वाजला}} rather than \textbf{\mr{वाजले}}? (\textbf{\mr{एक}} — one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vājtā]{\mr{वाजता} (vājtā) — \textquotedblleft{}at \_\_\_ o'clock\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:MR-C67-vajta}



\begin{quote}
Say it is one o'clock. Then say it is three o'clock, and hear the verb change.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{वाजता}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{दोन} \mr{वाजता} \mr{येतो}.} — \emph{mī don vājtā yeto.} — \textbf{I come at two o'clock.}
\end{quote}

Telling the time and putting something \emph{at} a time are two different jobs, and Marathi uses two different words for them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजले}} & it \textbf{is} two o'clock \\
\textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजता}} & \textbf{at} two o'clock \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one that never moves}]
\textbf{\mr{वाजले}} counted with you — \textbf{\mr{वाजला}} after one, \textbf{\mr{वाजले}} after the rest.

\textbf{\mr{वाजता} does not.} It is \textbf{\mr{वाजता}} after every number there is:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{वाजता}} & at one \\
\textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजता}} & at two \\
\textbf{\mr{बारा} \mr{वाजता}} & at twelve \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the harder-looking half of the clock is the easier one. And the whole phrase then goes where every time word on this track goes — \textbf{early, in front of the verb}, exactly where \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} sat.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ek vājtā}, \emph{don vājtā}, \emph{bārā vājtā}
  \item \emph{mī don vājtā yeto}
  \item the difference between \emph{don vājle} and \emph{don vājtā}
  \item the same sentence with a part of the day instead of a number
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \emph{at four o'clock}? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{चार} \mr{वाजता}}}.) Does \textbf{\mr{वाजता}} change after \mr{एक}? (\textbf{No} — only \textbf{\mr{वाजले}} does that.) And where does the phrase sit? (\textbf{In front of the verb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghaḍyāḷ]{(the clock) — from cold}

\label{lesson:MR-R67-clock-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Ask somebody the time, then answer yourself with one o'clock and with six o'clock.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words, one of which counts}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{telling it} & \textbf{placing something at it} \\
\midrule
one & \textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{वाजला}} & \textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{वाजता}} \\
two & \textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजले}} & \textbf{\mr{दोन} \mr{वाजता}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Only the left column moves, and only for \textbf{\mr{एक}}. The right column is one word for every hour on the clock.

This chapter added \textbf{no new numbers}. You had all twelve already, and until now the only thing you could do with them was count. The clock is what they were for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kitī vājle?}
  \item the hours from one to five, told
  \item the same hours, placed — \emph{ek vājtā … pāc vājtā}
  \item \emph{mī dahā vājtā yeto}
  \item which of the two words ever changes, and after which number
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask the time. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{वाजले}?}}) Say it is one o'clock. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{एक} \mr{वाजला}}}.) Say \emph{at eleven o'clock}. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{अकरा} \mr{वाजता}}}.) How many new numbers did this chapter teach you? (\textbf{None} — you had them all.)
\end{tcolorbox}
